prayer: Lord, I want to understand things that are sometimes beyond my understanding. I want answers, certainty, and the ability to make things turn out the way I believe they should. Help me recognize when the gifts You have given me become reasons to rely only upon myself. Keep my heart childlike—open enough to receive You, humble enough to need You, and willing to surrender the sovereignty that belongs only to You. I do not need to see everything You see. Let knowing You be enough. Amen.
theme: Surrendering control to God; trusting God when we do not understand; Job's encounter with God; becoming childlike in faith; humility, self-reliance, spiritual dependence, and recognizing God's sovereignty.
opening: Maybe surrender is not giving something up. Maybe it is recognizing what was never ours to hold.
body:
Job finally answers God.
After all of his questions, his suffering, his pleading to understand what he had done and why this had happened to him, God spoke to Job from the storm. But He never really answered Job's questions. Instead, God asked questions of His own—questions Job could not possibly answer.
Yesterday I wondered why.
Today Job seems to understand.
“I have dealt with great things that I do not understand; things too wonderful for me, which I cannot know.”
I don't think Job is apologizing simply because he questioned God. He had every reason to cry out. He had lost nearly everything. He wanted to know why. He wanted God to show him what he had done to deserve what was happening.
But after hearing God, something changes.
Job realizes how little he can actually see.
He says, “I had heard of you by word of mouth, but now my eye has seen you.”
That line feels enormous.
Job had known about God. He was already a faithful man. But now he has encountered God. And strangely, that encounter doesn't give Job the answers he had been demanding. God never explains the conversation that began Job's suffering. He never lays everything out so Job can finally say, Oh, now I understand.
Job still doesn't see what God sees.
He sees God.
And somehow that changes what he needs to know.
Job says he disowns what he has said and repents. I struggled with what exactly he is disowning. Is it all the questions? The why me? The pleading for God to show him what he had done? I don't think asking those questions was the problem.
Maybe what Job releases is the authority he had unknowingly given himself to judge what he could not possibly understand.
That is different.
There is something in us that wants to understand. We want things to make sense. We gather information, solve problems, make plans, anticipate what might happen and try to prepare for it. These are not bad things. God gave us minds capable of doing them.
But somewhere along the way, capability can become something else.
Sovereignty.
I can handle this.
I should be able to handle this.
If I know enough, plan enough, work hard enough and understand enough, I should be able to make this turn out correctly.
Maybe that is what has to be surrendered.
Not ourselves. Not our intelligence. Not our responsibility. Not even our questions.
The sovereignty we were never given.
Then the seventy-two return to Jesus in today's Gospel, amazed by what they have accomplished.
“Lord, even the demons are subject to us because of your name.”
They have actually done extraordinary things. Jesus gave them real authority and they experienced its power. I can imagine how astonishing that must have felt.
But Jesus redirects them almost immediately.
Do not rejoice because the spirits are subject to you. Rejoice because your names are written in heaven.
Almost as if to say: Do not confuse the gift with its Source.
Then Jesus rejoices and praises the Father because these things have been hidden from the wise and learned and revealed to the childlike.
The childlike.
Yesterday Jesus placed a child before His disciples when they wanted to know who was greatest. Today He returns to the childlike again.
I keep thinking about what happens to us as we grow up.
A child begins completely dependent. A child receives. A child trusts before understanding everything. The mind and heart are still open in a way that adulthood slowly changes.
Growing up requires us to become capable. We learn to care for ourselves, make decisions, solve problems and become responsible. Eventually a child leaves home precisely because he or she no longer needs a parent to do everything.
But maybe something dangerous can happen spiritually if we carry that same progression into our relationship with God.
We begin to think spiritual maturity means needing Him less.
We become knowledgeable. Experienced. Capable. We learn how the world works. And somewhere in all of that, the self can quietly take the place that once belonged to God.
Not because we stop believing in Him.
Because we begin believing so much in ourselves.
Maybe this is why Jesus doesn't say these things are revealed to the unintelligent. He says they are revealed to the childlike.
There is a difference.
Being childlike isn't about knowing less. It is being able to receive what we cannot give ourselves.
And Jesus goes even further. He says no one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him.
Even knowing God is received.
We cannot study enough to possess Him. We cannot reason our way into mastery of Him. We cannot become wise enough to stand above Him and finally understand how everything works.
He reveals Himself.
That brings me back to Job.
“I had heard of you by word of mouth, but now my eye has seen you.”
Maybe Job finally stopped needing to understand everything because he encountered the One who does.
He didn't become less intelligent.
He became humble.
And maybe humility is not thinking less of ourselves. Maybe it is finally understanding where our authority ends.
There are things that belong to us. We think, choose, work, create, question and act. God gave us those abilities.
But sovereignty belongs to God.
That may be why becoming childlike is so difficult for adults. We spend much of our lives learning independence, only to discover that spiritual maturity asks us to recognize how dependent we have always been.
Not helpless.
Dependent.
Job doesn't disappear when he surrenders. The seventy-two don't lose their gifts when Jesus redirects them. The wise do not have to become foolish.
We simply stop occupying a place that was never ours.
Maybe that is surrender.
Not abandoning ourselves.
Not refusing to think.
Not pretending we have no questions.
Just finally releasing the sovereignty we were never given.
Job never got to see what God sees.
He saw God.
And somehow, that was enough.
title: He saw God.
